entry: Main growth tissue in the stems and roots of many plants with secondary growth, notably dicots such as [[Oak|oak trees]] and [[Gymnosperm|gymnosperms]] such as [[Pine|pine trees]]. It produces secondary xylem inward, toward the pith, and secondary phloem outward, toward the [[Bark (botany)|bark]]; generally more xylem than phloem is produced. In woody plants it forms a continuous cylinder of unspecialized [[Meristem|meristem]] cells. Unlike xylem and phloem, it does not transport water, minerals or food. Its activity is regulated by signaling networks involving [[Plant hormone|hormones]] such as auxin, ethylene and cytokinins. Auxin stimulates mitosis and cell production, and plants lacking it show reduced growth of the vascular bundles. The cambium is absent from several angiosperm lineages, including the monocots, and successful grafting requires that the cambia of rootstock and scion be aligned.

Complex conducting tissue in vascular plants, consisting of xylem and phloem. These tissues transport water, minerals and nutrients throughout the plant, and their cells are long and slender, somewhat like pipes. Vascular tissue is arranged in strands called vascular bundles, which also contain supporting and protective cells. In stems and roots, xylem lies toward the interior and phloem toward the exterior. Between them is the [[Vascular cambium|vascular cambium]], a meristem that divides to form new xylem and phloem, increasing the girth of the plant. In [[Tree|trees]] and other woody plants, a separate cork cambium forms cork that protects the surface and reduces water loss. In [[Leaf|leaves]], xylem faces the upper surface and phloem the lower, which is why [[Aphid|aphids]] are typically found on the undersides of leaves.

Russian ballet dancer and choreographer of Polish ancestry. Regarded as the greatest male dancer of the early 20th century, he was associated with the Ballets Russes and its impresario Sergei Diaghilev. He choreographed influential ballets including *L'après-midi d'un faune* (1912), *Le Sacre du Printemps* (1913), *Jeux* (1913) and *Till Eulenspiegel* (1916). Celebrated for his virtuosity and leaps, he could dance en pointe, a rare skill for male dancers of the time. Born in Kiev, Russian Empire (now Kyiv, Ukraine), he trained at the Imperial Ballet School in St Petersburg. From 1919 his mental illness, diagnosed as [[Schizophrenia|schizophrenia]], ended his public career, and he spent much of the rest of his life in and out of psychiatric hospitals. He died in London.

Indian Buddhist monk and scholar (fl. 4th–5th century CE). He wrote a commentary on the Abhidharma from the perspectives of the Sarvāstivāda and Sautrāntika schools. His *Abhidharmakośakārikā* remains a major source for Abhidharma study in Tibetan and East Asian [[Buddhism|Buddhism]]. After converting to [[Mahayana|Mahayana]] Buddhism under the influence of his half-brother Asanga, he co-founded the Yogacara school. His verses set out its doctrine of "appearance only", described as a form of epistemological [[Idealism|idealism]] close to the transcendental idealism of [[Immanuel Kant]]. He also wrote commentaries, works on logic and devotional poetry. He is regarded as the second patriarch of Jōdo Shinshū and the 21st patriarch of Chan Buddhism.

Landlocked sovereign city-state in southern Europe, enclaved within [[Rome]], Italy. It is the seat of the [[Holy See]], the central authority of the Catholic Church, and an absolute monarchy under the pope, who is elected by the College of Cardinals. With an area of 0.49 sq km and a population of about 882, it is the smallest country by area and the least populous. Catholic tradition holds that Saint Peter was crucified on Vatican Hill. The Lateran Treaty of 1929 established the modern state, settling the Roman Question raised when the Kingdom of Italy captured Rome in 1870. Its sites include [[St. Peter's Basilica|St. Peter's Basilica]], the [[Sistine Chapel|Sistine Chapel]], the Apostolic Palace and the [[Vatican Museums|Vatican Museums]], and it is a World Heritage Site. The state uses the euro, issues its own coins and is a de facto member of the [[Schengen Area|Schengen Area]]. The Holy See maintains relations with 180 states and is an observer at the [[United Nations|United Nations]].

Public museums of Vatican City, housing collections assembled by the [[Catholic Church]] and the papacy. [[Pope Julius II]] founded them in the early 16th century. They hold roughly 70,000 works, of which 20,000 are on display, including several of the best-known Roman sculptures. The visitor route passes the [[Sistine Chapel]], decorated by [[Michelangelo]], and the *Stanze* decorated by [[Raphael]]. The collection grew from *Laocoön and His Sons*, discovered in 1506 and displayed at the Vatican a month later. The *Pinacoteca Vaticana*, opened in 1932, holds paintings by Giotto, [[Leonardo da Vinci]], [[Titian]] and Caravaggio. A Collection of Modern Religious Art, added in 1973, includes works by Vincent van Gogh, Paul Gauguin and Pablo Picasso. In 2024 the museums had 6.8 million visitors, second among the world's art museums only to the [[Louvre]].

Genre of variety entertainment popular in the United States and Canada until the early 1930s. A typical bill comprised unrelated acts such as comedians, [[Acrobatics|acrobats]], jugglers, [[Magic (illusion)|magicians]], singers, trained animals and [[Harry Houdini|escape artists]]. Vaudeville developed from the concert saloon, minstrelsy and burlesque, and was called "the heart of American show business." Its decline accelerated in the late 1920s as sound films and radio offered cheaper entertainment. The origin of the name is uncertain; it is often linked to the Vau de Vire, a Normandy valley known for drinking songs.

Branch of mathematics concerned with the differentiation and integration of vector fields, primarily in three-dimensional Euclidean space. The term is sometimes used as a synonym for [[Multivariable calculus|multivariable calculus]], which also covers partial differentiation and multiple integration. Its differential operators, the gradient, divergence and curl, are written with the [[Del|del]] operator. Its integral theorems generalize the [[Fundamental theorem of calculus|fundamental theorem of calculus]] to higher dimensions. It is used extensively in physics and engineering, notably for [[Electromagnetic field|electromagnetic fields]], gravitational fields and fluid flow. The subject grew out of [[Quaternion|quaternions]] near the end of the 19th century, when [[Josiah Willard Gibbs|J. Willard Gibbs]] and Oliver Heaviside shaped it. In its standard form using the [[Cross product|cross product]], it does not generalize to higher dimensions, unlike geometric algebra.

Linear algebraic structure in which vectors may be added and scaled by elements of a [[Field (mathematics)|field]], called scalars. Vector spaces generalize [[Euclidean vector|Euclidean vectors]], which model quantities such as [[Force|force]] and [[Velocity|velocity]] that have both magnitude and direction. Together with matrices, they are fundamental to [[Linear algebra|linear algebra]]. Real and complex vector spaces, whose scalars are real or complex numbers, are the most common. A vector space is characterized by its dimension, the number of independent directions it contains; it is finite-dimensional if that dimension is a [[Natural number|natural number]], and infinite-dimensional otherwise. Polynomial rings are countably infinite-dimensional, and many function spaces have the cardinality of the continuum as their dimension. Many vector spaces carry further structure, as with [[Hilbert space|Hilbert spaces]] and Banach spaces.

One of the six orthodox (āstika) schools of Hindu philosophy, also called Uttara Mīmāṃsā. Its name means "conclusion of the Vedas", and it originally referred to the [[Upanishads|Upanishads]]. Its traditions share a canon of three texts, the Upanishads, the Brahma Sutras and the [[Bhagavad Gita|Bhagavad Gita]], but interpret them differently. The main traditions are Bhedabheda, Advaita (non-dualism) and several [[Vishnu|Vishnu]]-centered traditions, including Dvaita (dualism) and Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism). Advaita emphasizes knowledge (jñana) over theistic devotion, and its monism attracted attention in the West partly through [[Swami Vivekananda|Swami Vivekananda]] and [[Ramana Maharshi|Ramana Maharshi]]. Most other major schools are related to [[Vaishnavism|Vaishnavism]] and emphasize devotion (bhakti) to God. Whereas Pūrva Mīmāṃsā deals with ritual, Vedanta addresses the relation between humans and the Divine or Absolute.

Period of early Indian history, c. 1500–500 BCE, marked by the composition of the [[Vedas|Vedas]] in northern India. The Vedas were composed and orally transmitted by speakers of an Old Indo-Aryan language who migrated into the northwest after the decline of the [[Indus Valley Civilisation|Indus Valley Civilisation]]. Early society was pastoral, organized in tribes rather than kingdoms, and patriarchal and patrilineal. From c. 1200–1000 BCE the culture spread east into the fertile western [[Ganges|Ganges]] Plain, where iron tools enabled forest clearing and settled farming. The later period saw the rise of towns and kingdoms, a complex social hierarchy, and the Kuru kingdom's codification of orthodox sacrificial ritual. Its end brought larger states called mahajanapadas and śramaṇa movements, including [[Jainism|Jainism]] and [[Buddhism|Buddhism]], that challenged Vedic orthodoxy. Vedic religion evolved into Brahmanical orthodoxy, one of the main constituents of the later Hindu synthesis.

Brightest star in the northern constellation [[Lyra|Lyra]], about 25 light-years from the Sun. Also designated Alpha Lyrae, it is the fifth-brightest star in the night sky and the second-brightest in the northern celestial hemisphere, after Arcturus. Vega was the first star other than the Sun to have its image and spectrum photographed, and one of the first whose distance was measured by [[Parallax|parallax]]. It served as a baseline for calibrating the photometric brightness scale. It is about a tenth the age of the Sun but 2.1 times as massive, and it rotates rapidly, at 236 km/s at the equator, so that its poles are hotter than its equator. It is a [[Variable star|variable star]]. A dust disk around it is analogous to the [[Kuiper belt|Kuiper belt]] of the [[Solar System|Solar System]], and James Webb Space Telescope observations show it to be exceptionally smooth. Vega was the northern pole star around 12000 BCE.

Practice of abstaining from the use of animal products, and the philosophy that rejects the commodity status of animals. Ethical veganism excludes all animal use, including food, clothing such as [[Leather|leather]] and [[Wool|wool]], entertainment such as [[Rodeo|rodeos]], [[Bullfighting|bullfighting]] and [[Zoo|zoos]], and animal testing. Dietary veganism refrains from meat, eggs, dairy and other animal-derived foods. The term was coined in 1944 by Donald and Dorothy Watson to distinguish it from [[Vegetarianism|vegetarianism]], which excludes meat but accepts dairy and eggs. Vegan diets risk deficiencies of [[Vitamin B12|vitamin B12]], iron, zinc, omega-3 fatty acids and protein, which may require fortification or supplementation. An estimated 79 million people, about 1% of the world's population, practice veganism, and interest in it rose significantly in the 2010s. Proponents cite lower greenhouse gas emissions and land use, though critics note that plant monocultures carry their own environmental costs.

Dark brown Australian spread made from leftover brewers' yeast extract with vegetable and spice additives. Cyril Callister developed it in [[Melbourne|Melbourne]] for the Fred Walker Company. Salty and malty with an [[Umami|umami]] flavor, it is typically eaten in small amounts on toast or sandwiches. It is high in B vitamins, and it is vegan and [[Halal|halal]]. After Fred Walker's death in 1935 the brand passed to Kraft Foods, and in 2017 it returned to Australian ownership when the Bega Group bought it from [[Mondelez International|Mondelez International]].

Fat extracted from seeds or other parts of edible plants, mostly composed of triglycerides. Olives were turned into oil in present-day [[Israel|Israel]] by 6000 BC, and vegetable oils were long used for lighting, cooking, medicine and lubrication. In 1780 Carl Wilhelm Scheele showed that fats contain glycerol, and Michel Eugène Chevreul later identified them as esters of [[Fatty acid|fatty acids]] and glycerol. Wilhelm Normann introduced the hydrogenation of liquid fats in 1901, which led to the global production of [[Margarine|margarine]] and vegetable shortening. In the United States, [[Procter & Gamble|Procter & Gamble]] marketed cottonseed-oil shortening, Crisco, as early as 1911. By the 1950s and 1960s soybean oil was the most popular vegetable oil in the U.S. Palm oil, a major commodity during the [[Industrial Revolution|Industrial Revolution]], became the basis of soap, and today vegetable oils are used in food, cosmetics, paints, lubricants and [[Biofuel|biofuel]].

Practice of abstaining from meat, including red meat, poultry, [[Seafood|seafood]], [[Insect|insects]] and the flesh of other animals. Some vegetarians also avoid all by-products of slaughter. Motives include respect for sentient animal life, codified in various religious beliefs and animal rights advocacy, as well as health, environmental, cultural and economic reasons. Variants include lacto-vegetarian (dairy), ovo-vegetarian (eggs) and lacto-ovo vegetarian diets, all of which include honey. The strictest form is [[Veganism|veganism]], which excludes all animal products. Vegetarians may develop a deficiency of [[Vitamin B12|vitamin B12]] unless they consume eggs, dairy or other reliable sources. The term was popularized by the founding of the Vegetarian Society in Manchester in 1847. Jainism made strict vegetarianism a mandate for all followers, and Pārśvanātha and [[Mahavira|Mahavira]], revived it in [[Jainism|Jain]] tradition between the 8th and 6th centuries BCE. Rishikesh, in [[India|India]], banned meat, fish and eggs in 1956.

Disorder of consciousness in which severe brain damage leaves partial arousal without true [[Consciousness|awareness]]. Patients may open their eyes and show sleep–wake cycles, but they lack [[Cognition|cognitive]] function. Unlike a [[Coma|coma]], which lacks both awareness and wakefulness, it is a chronic condition. After four weeks it is termed a persistent vegetative state, which is classified as permanent three months after a nontraumatic [[Brain injury|brain injury]] in the U.S. (six months in the U.K.), or one year after a traumatic injury. In the U.S., the persistent diagnosis can support a judicial request to end life support, a practice that has generated controversy. Because "vegetative" carries negative connotations, the term unresponsive wakefulness syndrome is sometimes preferred.

Cloth worn to cover the head or face, or hung over an object of significance. Veiling has a long history in European, Asian and African societies and has been prominent in [[Judaism|Judaism]], [[Christianity|Christianity]] and [[Islam|Islam]]. It is especially associated with women and sacred objects, although in some cultures men are expected to veil. The earliest attested reference is in a Middle Assyrian law code of between 1400 and 1100 BC, which made veiling a marker of rank and forbade it to prostitutes and female slaves. In [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]], respectable women were expected to conceal themselves from strangers. Roman matrons veiled to show modesty and chastity, and Roman brides wore a deep yellow veil called the *flammeum*. Today veiling persists in religious dress, such as the [[Hijab|hijab]], and in [[Wedding|wedding customs]]. It remains contested: Iran has enforced mandatory veiling since its 1979 revolution, while France has banned face coverings in public since 2010.

Blood vessel that carries blood toward the heart. Most veins carry deoxygenated blood from the tissues back to the heart, while pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs. Veins have thinner walls and wider lumens than arteries, so they hold more blood, and nearly 70% of the body's blood is in the veins at any time. Medium and large veins contain one-way valves that prevent backflow, and in the legs [[Muscle contraction|muscle contraction]] helps drive blood back to the heart. Veins lie close to the skin, and those that look blue owe their color to light scattering in the skin and visual processing rather than to the actual color of venous blood. Venules, the smallest veins, collect blood from [[Capillary|capillaries]] and merge into larger veins that empty into the right atrium of the [[Heart|heart]].

Brand name, now often used generically, for [[Fastener|hook-and-loop fasteners]] that bond two surfaces with tiny hooks and soft loops. Swiss engineer George de Mestral conceived the idea in 1941 after noticing how burrs clung to his clothing and his dog's fur. The name combines the French words for velvet and hook. Industry leaders rejected the idea in [[Lyon|Lyon]], then a weaving center, and cotton strips wore out quickly, so de Mestral turned to synthetic fibers. The fasteners separate when peeled apart, often with a distinctive ripping sound.

Genus of small dromaeosaurid dinosaurs of the Late Cretaceous, found in Asia. Two species are recognized: *V. mongoliensis*, from [[Mongolia|Mongolia]], and *V. osmolskae*, named in 2008 from skull material from China. Its length was about 1.5–2.07 m and its weight 14.1–19.7 kg, roughly the size of a turkey, far smaller than the reptiles of the *Jurassic Park* films. It was a bipedal, [[Feather|feathered]] carnivore with a long tail and an enlarged sickle-shaped claw on each hindfoot. Its first [[Skull|skull]] was found in 1923 during an [[American Museum of Natural History|American Museum of Natural History]] expedition to the [[Gobi Desert|Gobi Desert]], and the genus was named in 1924. The famous "Fighting Dinosaurs" [[Fossil|fossil]], found in 1971 by a Polish-Mongolian team, preserves a Velociraptor in combat with a *Protoceratops*.

Honoring of deceased people, especially ancestors, based on love and respect and often on the belief that the dead continue to exist and may influence the living. Ancestor veneration typically seeks the continued well-being and favor of the ancestors, and sometimes their help. Its social role is to cultivate [[Kinship|kinship]] values such as filial piety, family loyalty and continuity of the lineage. It is distinct from the worship of a deity: in Confucian-influenced societies, expressing filial piety often matters more than asking for favors. In much of Africa, ancestors are prayed to and sacrificed to, and may become minor deities. Some Christian churches venerate saints as intercessors with [[God|God]], and the [[Catholic Church|Catholic Church]] also prays for departed souls in [[Purgatory|Purgatory]]. Other religious groups regard veneration of the dead as [[Idolatry|idolatry]] and a [[Sin|sin]]. Ancestor veneration appears in all documented human cultures, and one hypothesis holds that it helped coordinate groups during human evolution.

Region of northeastern Italy (pop., 2026: 4,857,460), with its capital at [[Venice|Venice]]. Part of the [[Roman Empire|Roman Empire]] until the 5th century AD, it later belonged to the [[Republic of Venice|Republic of Venice]] until 1797. After the [[Napoleonic Wars|Napoleonic Wars]] and the [[Congress of Vienna|Congress of Vienna]], it was re-annexed to the Austrian Empire and joined the [[Kingdom of Italy|Kingdom of Italy]] in 1866. Once a land of mass emigration, Veneto is today one of the greatest immigrant-receiving regions in Italy, with foreign-born residents making up 13.9% of the population.

Federal presidential republic on the northern coast of [[South America|South America]] (pop., 2025: 31.8 million), with its capital at [[Caracas|Caracas]]. Colonized by Spain in 1522, it declared independence in 1811 and joined the first federal Republic of Colombia, known as [[Gran Colombia|Gran Colombia]], before separating as a sovereign country in 1830. From 1958 it had a series of democratic governments, but economic shocks in the 1980s and 1990s brought unrest. [[Hugo Chávez|Hugo Chávez]] was elected in 1998, beginning the Bolivarian Revolution. Venezuela has the world's largest known oil reserves, and oil came to dominate its exports and government revenue. Poverty began to rise rapidly in mid- to late 2014, and the 2013, 2018 and 2024 presidential elections were widely disputed. In 2026 U.S. forces captured Nicolás Maduro, and Vice President Delcy Rodríguez was sworn in as acting president. Critics describe the government as authoritarian, and some observers describe the country as a puppet state of the U.S. in its finances and domestic policy. Hyperinflation, shortages and crime have contributed to a refugee crisis in which more than 7.9 million people have fled the country.

City (pop., 2026: 249,385), capital of [[Veneto|Veneto]] in northeastern Italy. Built on 126 islands in the shallow Venetian Lagoon and linked by 472 bridges, it was the capital of the [[Republic of Venice|Republic of Venice]] from 810 to 1797. A major financial and maritime power in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, it was a staging area for the [[Crusades|Crusades]] and the Battle of Lepanto, and a center of commerce in silk, grain and spice. [[Napoleon|Napoleon]] ended the republic in 1797, and the city became part of the [[Kingdom of Italy|Kingdom of Italy]] in 1866. Venice was the birthplace of Baroque composers [[Antonio Vivaldi|Antonio Vivaldi]] and Tomaso Albinoni. The lagoon and city were inscribed as a [[UNESCO|UNESCO]] World Heritage Site in 1987, but overtourism, pollution, tide peaks and cruise ships threaten the city, and its listing has been under continuing review.
